overview: Totonac communities have lived across the coastal plains of Veracruz and the northern mountains of Puebla. Their history includes powerful centers such as Cempoala and enduring local identities, rather than one unchanging empire. The imported 1492 to 1500 window is a map snapshot; its outline shows only part of a wider region. Totonac people and languages continue today.

periods.title: Late preconquest coastal centers
periods.summary: Cempoala was a major political and ceremonial center and later collected tribute under Mexica domination. Its population included Totonacs, Chinantecs and Zapotecs.

periods.title: Alliance and colonial rule
periods.summary: The alliance against the Mexica did not secure lasting freedom from colonial demands. Spanish authorities imposed new obligations and reorganized Indigenous jurisdictions.

periods.title: Living communities and renewed teaching
periods.summary: Community knowledge continues through language, arts, family relationships and education. The Totonac Centre for Indigenous Arts organizes teaching around specialized house-schools.

items.text: Cempoala gathered tribute from surrounding communities before Spanish arrival. INAH describes it as the head of roughly fifty towns with several ethnic affiliations. Totonac political influence therefore involved a diverse regional population, not a city inhabited by only one people.

In 1519, Cempoala’s leadership allied with Hernán Cortés against Mexica power. The choice arose within an existing struggle over tribute and domination. It was a political decision by Indigenous leaders whose communities had their own interests.

Water from the Actopan River was carried toward Cempoala by gravity. Drainage served houses and major buildings, while raised platforms helped adapt construction to low ground. The city’s planners had to think about where water would go after it arrived.

INAH describes ducts carrying wastewater from homes and buildings toward cultivated areas. This is unusually concrete evidence about urban sanitation and farming. It does not identify a particular toilet design, so the card cannot furnish every ancient bathroom.

The Building of the Little Faces preserves sculptural and painted decoration; El Pimiento has tiers ornamented with stone skulls. Their arrangement around open plazas shows how architecture shaped shared ceremonial space, alongside the less conspicuous infrastructure that supported households.

sections.title: Family, food and care in living traditions

items.text: INPI’s ethnographic account describes compadrazgo, ritual co-parenthood, as a network connecting personal and working relationships. Bonds formed around baptisms, marriages and funerals can extend mutual obligations beyond the immediate household. This is documented community life after Christianity’s arrival, not a universal preconquest rule.

The same account describes midwives caring for mothers during pregnancy and birth, with traditional knowledge including plants and temazcal steam baths. These are reported healing practices and beliefs; the evidence does not establish that every treatment was effective or used by every family.

A cultural inventory follows maize through a very practical sequence: kernels are prepared as nixtamal, ground on a metate or in a mill, and cooked as tortillas on a comal. Atoles and fermented maize drinks broaden the menu. A single crop can keep a kitchen remarkably busy.

In 2026, Papantla cook Micaela Simbrón Rodríguez of Mujeres de Humo shared Totonac cooking through pulacles, bocoles and molotes. Her work gives this heritage a named contemporary teacher, rather than leaving traditional food as an anonymous list of dishes.

sections.title: Learning, ceremony and a written greeting

items.text: The Totonac Centre for Indigenous Arts includes house-schools for pottery, textiles, healing, music and cooking. At the House of Elders, students learn the values surrounding creative work. Instruction in Totonac connects practical skill with language and community knowledge.

The center also links cultural teaching to replanting trees and other plants needed for artistic practice. Materials have to grow somewhere before a maker can use them. Protecting a craft can therefore include caring for the landscape that supplies it.

In the Voladores ceremony, four flyers descend on ropes while a fifth participant, the caporal, plays flute and drum from above. UNESCO describes it as a ritual expressing relations with nature and the spiritual world. Several peoples practice versions of it; it is especially associated with Totonac communities.

A modern written greeting in the central-northern Totonac variety Tutunakuj is “Tun Kuil’”, meaning “Good morning”. INALI publishes it with text and voice by Elías García Aparicio and the Spanish translation “Buenos días”. The Latin-letter spelling belongs to this documented variety, not to an invented ancient inscription.

ending.text: Totonac alliance with the Spaniards was followed by colonial religious and labor demands and the reorganization of local authorities. The end of earlier political arrangements did not end the people. Totonac communities, languages and institutions remain active; 1500 is merely the imported map endpoint.
